title: Police shooting death prompts soul-searching at city hall
subtitle: Staff who got to know frequent visitor Ian Pryce before his death seek ways to help other mentally ill people who show up at their door.
article: Holed up outside a Sherbourne St. apartment building, on the small wooden porch where he was about to die, Ian Pryce wasn't making much sense.

Engaged in a tense standoff with more than two dozen members of the Toronto police Emergency Task Force (ETF) in November 2013, Pryce insisted he be called "Frost." He claimed he was a police officer, then a judge. He was mumbling to himself.
But the 30-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia was perfectly coherent when he told ETF officers training their weapons on him to call a woman he thought could help.
He instructed police to contact Sherry-Ann Lotz, and then provided the correct phone number to reach her at City Hall, a coroner's inquest into Pryce's death heard this week.
"What's Sherry-Ann saying?" Pryce asked Toronto police, three minutes before he was fatally shot by two officers, according to audio played at the inquest.
Lotz was among the city hall staff Pryce befriended in the final eight weeks of his life, when he suddenly began making frequent trips to speak to city staff for reasons that were often unclear.

"He came initially with a city issue, a municipal issue, bedbugs - perhaps he felt safe coming here. I don't know why he continued to," Melissa Wong, who works for Kristyn Wong-Tam, Pryce's councillor, told the Star.

Lotz, then employed in Councillor Pam McConnell's office, bonded with Pryce in the early mornings, when he was waiting for Wong-Tam's staff to arrive. Early birds at city hall, the two would sometimes have coffee together.

Peter Rosenthal, the lawyer for Pryce's mother, Heather Thompson, believes Pryce began frequenting city hall partly for social reasons. "I guess he didn't have many people to really talk to," he said in an interview.

To staff in Wong-Tam's office, the soft-spoken and polite young man fast became a familiar face, someone they recognized as being mentally ill and in need of help. But despite efforts to connect him to the assistance he needed, they could not find a way to help Pryce.

His death, they say, highlights the need for more support for people in crisis, and for additional resources for city hall employees, some of whom regularly interact with people with mental health challenges.

"It never should have gotten to the point that day where he was shot. There should have been proper intervention weeks beforehand," said David Simor, a staff member at Wong-Tam's office who dealt extensively with Pryce.
"It terrifies me, the fact that Ian was here, in the seat of government, and he couldn't get help."
Pryce was killed on Nov. 13, 2013, when police attempted to apprehend him after learning a warrant was out for his arrest in connection with an assault.

Pryce fled the officers, then brought out a weapon they believed was a handgun, later determined to be a pellet gun. Photographs of the weapon show that, from a distance, it would look virtually identical to a handgun.
The ongoing coroner's inquest is now examining the factors that led to Pryce's death, including his extensive involvement with the mental health system.
The purpose of an inquest is not to assign guilt, but to identify the problems that contributed to the death. A jury is then asked to make recommendations to avoid deaths.

The inquest is also examining police actions taken prior to Pryce's death. On Friday, Rosenthal questioned a lead Emergency Task Force officer, Sgt. Oswald Veit, on the conduct of the officers involved in the standoff, including why no effort was in fact made to contact Lotz, the city hall employee.
"A man in a crisis situation like that, who gives you a name and number like that, is hoping for help from that person," Rosenthal said.

Veit responded by saying officers had limited time and didn't know who she was; she could have been an ex-girlfriend who wouldn't have been helpful, and that police "can't put someone like that in danger."
Lotz is scheduled to testify at the inquest next week. Reached by the Star on Friday, she declined to comment prior to giving her testimony.
During the weeks Pryce was coming to city hall, staff began noticing a change in his behaviour, shifting from relatively together and relaxed to increasingly disorganized.

"In those last few weeks, one sentence would not have any relationship to the next. It was a very broken stream of consciousness," said Tristan Downe-Dewdney, another staff member with Wong-Tam's office.

Staff went down various avenues to try to help him. He refused to provide information about his family, so they could not contact them for help. They attempted to connect him with housing agencies or Toronto Public Health, in the hope that they could put him in contact with a caseworker.
"We don't have a means to connect people with mental health services, other than 'You should go here, you should go to this place,' and giving them a phone number and address," Wong said.
They could not easily arrange for somebody to come to city hall and meet with Pryce. When they did, he would sometimes wait for hours.
Encouraging him to go see a doctor didn't work, and "the only other resort is the police," Wong said.
That's who was called on Sept. 27, 2013 - six weeks before Pryce's death - when he walked up to a city hall receptionist and asked if someone could help him purchase a gun.
He said he was feeling fearful, city hall staff said. Police responded, questioned him, then let him go.

In a December 2013 letter written by Wong-Tam to the then city manager, Wong-Tam asked for a review of the interactions Pryce had with staff in the six months before his death, to determine "what improvements can be made to training or resources for city staff." That review was never completed, Wong-Tam said.

Staff in her office have taken it upon themselves to make improvements. Downe-Dewdney, for instance, has arranged for mental health crisis training for some city hall employees, and is now working to set up training specifically for encounters with people with schizophrenia.

Rosenthal and staff from Wong-Tam's office say it would be helpful to create a position at city hall to deal exclusively with people in crisis who come in seeking help, someone with the skills to navigate the mental health system.
Something must be done, Wong-Tam wrote in her condolence motion at city hall soon after Pryce's death. He was failed by a system that is not equipped to serve his needs, she wrote.
"We must do better."
